summary: Describes an RTP payload format for the VP9 video codec, covering low-bitrate peer-to-peer uses to high-bitrate video conferences, with support for temporal and spatial scalability.

eli5.summary: VP9 video must be cut into small packets to travel the internet. This says how to cut and label them so they can be reassembled.

subtitle: How VP9 video is chopped into RTP packets, with layer labels so servers and receivers can handle scalable streams.

tldr.problem: VP9 video has to travel over RTP in packets. Conferencing systems also need to know which layer each packet belongs to, and what it depends on, so that layers can be dropped or switched.
tldr.mechanism: A VP9 payload descriptor at the start of each packet carries frame boundaries, a picture ID, layer indices and reference information, with an optional scalability structure that pre-declares resolutions and dependencies.
tldr.outcome: The format registers the media type video/vp9 with a 90 kHz clock, defines SDP parameters, and ties in with the Layer Refresh Request of RFC 9627.

facts.label: Reference frames
facts.value: Up to 8 kept, up to 3 used per frame

today: RFC 9628 is a Proposed Standard published in March 2025. It has not been obsoleted or updated, so it is the definition of the VP9 RTP payload format.

sections.title: Scope and Purpose
sections.content:
RFC 9628 specifies an RTP payload format for video encoded with the VP9 codec. The abstract says it supports uses from low-bitrate peer-to-peer calls to high-bitrate video conferences, and includes provisions for temporal and spatial scalability.

The RFC describes VP9 as developed by Google and the successor to VP8. Beyond compression gains, VP9 is designed so that spatially scalable encoding is possible. The payload format is for the codec as defined in the VP9 bitstream specification; use of RTP/AVPF (RFC 4585) is RECOMMENDED to handle network losses.
sections.eli5: This document explains how to put VP9 video into network packets so calls and video meetings can use it.

sections.title: Layers, Pictures and Dependencies
sections.content:
VP9 can keep up to eight reference frames, and any new frame can reference up to three. A frame may also use a reference of different size, between 1/16th and twice its own width and height. Together this lets an encoder build temporal, spatial and quality scalability without special scalable coding tools.

Temporal layers give different frame rates. Spatial layers give different resolutions, and quality layers give the same resolution at different quality; the RFC calls both spatial layers. Layer IDs are non-negative integers, with zero as the base. Layers MUST be encoded so that removing any layer and all higher ones along either dimension leaves a decodable stream.

A frame is one encoded VP9 frame at a given resolution or quality. A picture is all the frames at one instant. A spatial-layer S frame may depend on the S-1 frame of the same picture, flagged by the D bit.

Two modes describe dependencies between pictures. In flexible mode, each packet lists up to three reference indices, so structures can change dynamically. In non-flexible mode, a fixed repeating pattern called a Picture Group (PG) is declared in advance in the scalability structure. The encoder can switch modes only on the first packet of a keyframe with temporal-layer ID zero.
sections.eli5: A video can be made of layers, like a small picture, a bigger picture and an even bigger one. Each layer may lean on the one below it. The packet labels tell the receiver what leans on what.

sections.title: RTP Header and Payload Descriptor
sections.content:
After the RTP header comes a VP9 payload descriptor, then the VP9 payload. All integer fields are unsigned, in network octet order. In the RTP header, the marker bit MUST be 1 on the final packet of the highest spatial-layer frame (the last packet of the picture). The payload type is dynamic and mapped through SDP. The timestamp uses a 90 kHz clock, and all frames of one picture MUST share the same timestamp.

The first octet of the descriptor has the flags I P L F B E V Z:

  • I: a Picture ID is present.
  • P: the frame uses inter-picture prediction.
  • L: layer indices are present.
  • F: flexible mode.
  • B and E: start and end of a frame.
  • V: scalability structure data is present.
  • Z: not a reference for upper spatial layers, so a receiver aiming higher can discard it.

The Picture ID is 7 or 15 bits (chosen by the sender with the M bit), increases by one per picture, SHOULD start at a random number and MUST wrap. The layer index octet holds TID, a switching-up bit U, SID and the inter-layer dependency bit D. In non-flexible mode an extra TL0PICIDX octet tracks base temporal-layer pictures. In flexible mode, when P and F are both 1, one to three P_DIFF values give each reference as a relative Picture ID, and a P_DIFF of zero is invalid.

Frames are fragmented in sequence order from a packet with B set to one with E set. There is no finer-grained access to parts of a frame.
sections.eli5: Each packet starts with a small label. It says whether it is the start or end of a frame, which picture and layer it belongs to, and which earlier pictures it needs.

sections.title: The Scalability Structure
sections.content:
When the V bit is set, scalability structure (SS) data is included. It starts with N_S (number of spatial layers minus 1), a Y flag and a G flag. If Y is set, a 2-octet width and 2-octet height follow for each spatial layer. If G is set, N_G describes the pictures in a Picture Group. For each, the SS gives its temporal-layer ID, a switch-up bit and its P_DIFF references. The first picture in the PG MUST have TID zero.

For a stream sent with a fixed pattern, the SS data SHOULD be included in the first packet of every keyframe. It MUST only change on the picture that matches the first picture of the previous PG.

The RFC also gives an example with three spatial and three temporal layers, showing which of the codec's reference buffers each frame references and updates. It is built so the U bit can always be set.
sections.eli5: The structure is like a plan handed over at the start: how many sizes there are and which pictures depend on which. After that, packets can just point to the plan.

sections.title: Encoding for Scalability and Feedback
sections.content:
A scalable encoder must make sure a frame does not depend on a frame that might legitimately be removed. A frame that follows a removable frame MUST be encoded with error_resilient_mode set to true. For spatially scalable streams this means the base spatial layer; higher layers can leave it off if they are sent with inter-layer dependency.

Three RTCP feedback messages are covered:

  • RPSI (Reference Picture Selection Indication) lets a receiver signal a preferred reference after a loss, or acknowledge a correctly decoded reference. The message body is the 7- or 15-bit Picture ID.
  • FIR (RFC 5104): the sender MUST send a keyframe for spatial layer 0, then frames with no inter-picture prediction (P=0) for higher layers.
  • LRR (RFC 9627) asks for a single layer to be refreshed. The VP9 layer fields carry TID and SID. Encoders SHOULD set P to zero for a layer sync frame, and SHOULD include layer indices and reference fields in such packets so middleboxes can find the switch points.
sections.eli5: If a receiver loses track of the picture, it can tell the sender what it still has, ask for a full restart, or ask to restart just one layer.

sections.title: SDP Parameters and Media Type
sections.content:
Three optional parameters exist. max-fr is the maximum frame rate in frames per second the decoder can handle. max-fs is the maximum frame size in macroblocks. profile-id is the default VP9 profile (0 to 3); if absent, Profile 0 MUST be inferred. A receiver willing to receive media MUST give both max-fr and max-fs, and a receiver MUST ignore parameters it does not know.

In SDP the media name MUST be video, the encoding name VP9 and the clock rate 90000. In offer/answer, profile-id identifies the format configuration and MUST be used symmetrically, while max-fr and max-fs are declarative and describe each side's receiving capability.

The media type video/vp9 is registered with IANA and added to the RTP payload format media types registry with a 90000 Hz clock rate.
sections.eli5: Before a call, each side says how big and how fast a video it can handle, and which flavor of VP9 it uses, so the other side does not send more than it can take.

sections.title: Security and Congestion Control
sections.content:
The format inherits RTP's security considerations and those of the RTP profile in use. Applications SHOULD use appropriate strong security mechanisms. The RFC stresses that decoders must be robust against malicious or malformed payloads, since an overrun of allocated memory could lead to arbitrary code execution. It judges the format unlikely to be a denial-of-service threat through pathological data, and it has no active content.

Congestion control for RTP SHALL be used per RFC 3550. Media-aware network elements MAY use the payload descriptor to spot non-reference frames and discard them to ease congestion, but cannot do so if the stream is encrypted because the non-reference marker is encrypted.
sections.eli5: The video software must be careful with broken or hostile packets. If the packets are encrypted, helper boxes in the network cannot peek at labels to throw away unimportant pieces.
